items.question: Let l,r be arbitrary natural numbers, possibly zero. Let A be a real l by (2r) matrix whose columns are indexed by (bit,new bond) in Fin 2 × Fin r, and assume AAᵀ=I_l. Define M(v)=∑_a v_a² for real row vectors. Proposition P: for every real row boundary v in R^l, M(vA)=M(v). Decide P and explain the input/output orientation and the role of normalization.
items.reference_answer: P is true for every real v; no unit-norm premise is needed. The output coordinates of vA are (bit,new bond). Expanding their squared mass gives ∑_{a,c} v_a v_c ∑_out A_{a,out}A_{c,out}. The inner sum is (AAᵀ)_{a,c}=δ_{a,c}, so the result is ∑_a v_a². In circuit notation U_{out,a}=A_{a,out} viewed in C, so U has 2r output rows and l input columns; U†U=I_l. For real inputs U times the column v equals the transpose/cast of vA because scalar multiplication commutes. A normalized output follows only when M(v)=1. The mass identity itself includes arbitrary norm and the empty-index cases.

rubric.criterion: Expands the squared mass or equivalent Gram contraction and uses AAᵀ=I_l.
Identifies old bond as input and (bit,new bond) as output; circuit U is the transposed/cast core.
States equality for arbitrary signed v with no M(v)=1 premise.
Distinguishes mass preservation from automatic unit normalization.

items.question: Let l,r,A and M be as follows: A is a real matrix with old-bond rows Fin l and output columns Fin 2 × Fin r, AAᵀ=I_l, and M(w)=∑_i w_i². Proposition P: every real row boundary v satisfies M(vA)=1. No further assumption on v is supplied. Decide P, and if it fails give exact dimensions, entries and a boundary, then state the minimum extra premise or corrected conclusion.
items.reference_answer: P is false. Take l=r=1 and A=[1,0], with columns (0,0),(1,0), and v=[2]. Then AAᵀ=[1], whereas vA=[2,0] has mass 4. The source interface gives M(vA)=M(v), which explains this failure without appealing to numerical rounding. Keep the arbitrary-input domain and replace 1 by M(v), or explicitly restrict v by M(v)=1. One must not silently add that normalization premise to a claim about every real v.

Calculates a nonunit output mass, e.g. 4 for v=[2].
Diagnoses preservation of the existing norm rather than normalization of arbitrary input.
Offers corrected equality for arbitrary v or explicitly states M(v)=1 as the additional premise.

items.question: Let A be a real l × (2r) core, A_{a,(b,j)}, where a is the old bond, b∈Fin 2 the emitted bit and j∈Fin r the new bond. Assume AAᵀ=I_l. Form V with output rows ordered (new bond,bit) by V_{(j,b),a}=A_{a,(b,j)} as a complex number. Proposition P: V†V=I_l for arbitrary natural l,r. Decide P; explain exactly which register is permuted and whether a new normalization assumption is needed.
items.reference_answer: P is true. V is (2r) × l: only its output labels have changed from (b,j) to (j,b). For old-bond columns a,c, (V†V)_{a,c}=∑_{j,b} A_{a,(b,j)}A_{c,(b,j)}. Reindex the finite sum using the bijection (j,b)↔(b,j). It becomes (AAᵀ)_{a,c}=δ_{a,c}. Realness removes conjugation. Thus an output-register permutation preserves column orthonormality. It neither exchanges input and output nor asserts equality of amplitudes at unchanged labels; the coordinate equation is V_{(j,b),a}=U_{(b,j),a}. No boundary normalization is involved, and zero dimensions remain allowed when the premise is satisfiable.

rubric.criterion: States V has output index (new bond,bit) and input index old bond.
Expands V†V and performs the explicit output-pair swap bijection.
Uses realness and AAᵀ=I_l to conclude the input Gram identity.
Explains that preserved isometry does not imply unchanged coordinate entries or additional normalization.

items.question: There is one old-bond basis vector, one two-level physical bit and one two-level new bond. Let A be a real 1 × 4 row, indexed by (bit,new bond), with AAᵀ=[1]. Define U_{(b,j),0}=A_{0,(b,j)} as complex entries, and define V_{(j,b),0}=A_{0,(b,j)}. Both ordered output sets happen to be Fin 2 × Fin 2. Proposition P: V=U as matrices with the same literal pair labels, for every such A. Decide P, including an exact witness if needed and the correct relationship between entries.
items.reference_answer: P is false even though both matrices have orthonormal columns. Put A_{0,(1,0)}=1 and every other entry 0. Its row mass is one. U is supported on output label (1,0), whereas V is supported on label (0,1). At literal label (0,1), V has entry 1 and U has entry 0, so V≠U. The valid relation is V_{(j,b),0}=U_{(b,j),0}; as operators, V is obtained by applying the output-register swap permutation to U. Swapping factors preserves the Gram matrix, but the output state generally changes when read at fixed pair labels.

rubric.criterion: Provides any exact real 1-by-4 row satisfying AAᵀ=[1] under the stated indexing.
Exhibits a fixed-label entry or an equivalent exact mathematical certificate showing V differs from U; any admissible witness is accepted.
Distinguishes isometry from coordinate-wise invariance.
States the swapped-label relationship or output-permutation composition.

items.question: For arbitrary natural l,r let A be a real l × (2r) matrix with AAᵀ=I_l. Let U have output rows (bit,new bond)∈Fin 2 × Fin r and input columns a∈Fin l, with U_{out,a}=A_{a,out} embedded in C. Proposition P: UU†=I_(Fin 2 × Fin r). Decide P; give an exact finite witness if it fails and explain the dimension and physical-register issue.
items.reference_answer: P is false. With l=r=1, take A=[1,0]. Then U=(1,0)ᵀ is a 2 × 1 embedding. U†U=[1] on the one-dimensional input, but UU†=diag(1,0), not I_2: the output (bit=1,new bond=0) diagonal entry is 0 rather than 1. Column orthonormality guarantees an isometric embedding of the input into the output; it does not imply surjectivity onto the entire output space. UU† is the orthogonal projection onto the range of U. For a square U, U†U=I does imply UU†=I in finite dimensions, but rectangular cores in this statement are not square in general.

items.question: Let l,r be arbitrary natural numbers and A a real core indexed by old bond a and output (bit,new bond), with AAᵀ=I_l. Define U_{out,a}=A_{a,out} in C and define Q=UU†, a square matrix on the output space. Proposition P: Q²=Q. Decide P and explain whether this condition asserts Q=I or unitary state preparation on the full output register.
items.reference_answer: P is true. The source orientation gives U†U=I_l. By associativity, Q²=(UU†)(UU†)=U(U†U)U†=UI_lU†=UU†=Q. Also Q†=Q follows from conjugate-transpose rules, and Q fixes each vector Ux while mapping every output vector into range(U). Hence it is the orthogonal projection onto that range. Idempotence alone does not say Q=I; the rectangular embedding U=(1,0)ᵀ yields Q=diag(1,0). The displayed Lean target certifies idempotence; the Hermitian/range explanation and any circuit completion claim have separate scope. No additional normalized state boundary is needed.

rubric.criterion: Invokes or derives the correctly oriented U†U=I_l.
Derives Q²=Q by a valid argument using the isometry condition, such as U(U†U)U† or the fact that Q maps into and fixes range(U).
States idempotence without inferring Q=I.
Explains the range projection meaning and its boundary; does not claim an efficient completion/compiler.

items.question: Let f be any real amplitude table on n+1 binary wires, with no positivity or normalization assumption. For an n-bit prefix b define m(f)(b)=sqrt(f(b,0)²+f(b,1)²), where (b,v) means appending last bit v. For any table g define N(g)=∑_w g(w)². Proposition P: N(m(f))=N(f) for all natural n and all such f. Decide P and explain the precise normalization invariant it supplies to a recursive loader.
items.reference_answer: P is true for arbitrary signed and unnormalized real f. The radicand is nonnegative, so m(f)(b)²=f(b,0)²+f(b,1)². Sum over prefixes. Every (n+1)-bit word is uniquely (b,v) with v∈{0,1}, and reindexing along this bijection yields N(m(f))=N(f). Therefore N(f)=1 propagates to the marginal whenever it is actually assumed, and the equality also preserves any other squared norm. This is a nonlinear length-table reduction; it does not retain signed amplitudes or itself specify a linear quantum evolution. A recursive preparation circuit uses additional signed splitting data to reconstruct them.

rubric.criterion: Uses nonnegativity of the sum of two squares to square the square root.
Reindexes all full words by prefix and last bit, including both last-bit cases.
Retains arbitrary signed and unnormalized source domain.
States conditional unit-normalization propagation and distinguishes the nonlinear table reduction from a linear state map.

items.question: On one binary wire identify a real table f with the pair (f(0),f(1)). Its zero-wire marginal m(f) is the one-entry table with value sqrt(f(0)²+f(1)²). Addition of tables is entrywise. Proposition P: for every real one-wire f,g, m(f+g)=m(f)+m(g). Decide P; explain what your result says about treating the norm-preserving marginal pass as a linear circuit isometry.
items.reference_answer: P is false. Take f=(1,0), g=(-1,0). Then f+g=(0,0), so m(f+g)=0, but m(f)=m(g)=1 and m(f)+m(g)=2. All values are exact; each of the two inputs separately has squared norm one. Thus norm preservation does not imply additivity or a linear isometry. The marginal loses sign information (m(-f)=m(f)); it is a nonlinear preprocessing map on amplitude descriptions. The correct source claim is squared-norm equality for each table, not linear evolution under addition. Even restricting to normalized inputs would not define a linear subspace; unit-norm inputs in this witness already expose the inappropriate linear-map claim.

rubric.criterion: Provides any exact real one-wire tables f and g with a demonstrable failure of marginal additivity.
Checks the two marginal expressions or an equivalent exact inequality and proves they differ; the reference pair and values are examples rather than required answers.
Distinguishes pointwise norm preservation from additivity/linearity and sign retention.
Repairs to the squared-norm invariant and explains why this preprocessing map cannot itself be the linear circuit state-action.

items.question: Use exact complex amplitudes and column vectors. For finite sets C, S, X and a family p assigning a bijection p_s:X→X to every s∈S, the basis is A=C×(S×X). The controlled map is F_p(c,(s,x))=(c,(s,p_s(x))). The SELECT matrix is U_p(r,k)=1 if r=F_p(k), and 0 otherwise. Thus coefficient c and selector s are preserved, and no ancilla is added. All statements are exact equalities of matrices over ℂ; finite sets may be empty unless a concrete set is specified. Put D=X×(C×S), and let J(c,(s,x))=(x,(c,s)). Define U'_p(r,k)=U_p(J⁻¹(r),J⁻¹(k)). Proposition: for every C,S,X,p and every r,k∈D, U'_p(r,k)=1 exactly when r=(p_{k.2.2}(k.1),(k.2.1,k.2.2)), and it is 0 otherwise. Decide whether the stated proposition is valid under exactly the supplied assumptions. Give a mathematical reason. If it is invalid, give an exact finite basis witness and state a repair; distinguish the original proposition from the repair.
items.reference_answer: J⁻¹(x,(c,s))=(c,(s,x)). Therefore J F_p J⁻¹(x,(c,s))=(p_s(x),(c,s)). Reindexing both matrix indices gives exactly the proposed indicator. The inverse on D is (x,(c,s))↦(p_s⁻¹(x),(c,s)); the selector is the third component in D, and both c and s remain preserved. The proof is uniform in all finite C,S,X, including empty carriers.

rubric.criterion: Reconstructs J inverse and the conjugated controlled action without moving the control to the wrong register.
Identifies the coefficient and selector components that are preserved.
Derives the exact row/column indicator amplitude, including the zero case.

assumptions: k is an arbitrary natural number, including zero; p and q are arbitrary real-coefficient polynomials, including the zero polynomial.
For every natural j with 0≤j≤k, the j-th ordinary derivatives of p and q agree at -1 and also agree at 0.
Both p and q have degree at most 2k+1 under the stated zero-polynomial convention.
conventions: Real polynomials and ordinary derivatives; the zero polynomial is allowed and satisfies the nonnegative degree bounds.
items.question: Proposition P: for every natural number k and all real-coefficient polynomials p and q, if both have degree at most 2k+1, and all their ordinary derivatives of orders 0 through k agree at -1 and agree at 0, then p=q. Is P valid under the assumptions and conventions below?
items.reference_answer: P is valid. Set d=p-q. Equality of all ordinary derivatives through k at a point a means that (x-a)^(k+1) divides d: the degree-j Taylor coefficient is d^(j)(a)/j!, and the factorial is nonzero over the reals. Thus (x+1)^(k+1) and x^(k+1) both divide d. The two factors are coprime since x+1 and x differ by the unit1, so their product divides d. This product has degree2k+2, whereas d has degree at most2k+1. A nonzero multiple cannot have smaller degree than its divisor, so d=0 and p=q. If d=0 already, this last conclusion is immediate. The assertion includes k=0 and zero input polynomials; it asserts uniqueness, not existence.

rubric.criterion: Respects arbitrary real polynomials, natural k including0, both degree bounds, exactly endpoints-1/0 and ordinary derivatives j=0..k.
Justifies how the two endpoint jet constraints control the polynomial difference, through multiplicity/divisibility, root counting or an equivalent rigorous uniqueness argument.
Correctly uses the stated degree bound to exclude a nonzero difference, or gives a complete mathematically equivalent uniqueness proof under that bound.
Proves the full universally quantified conclusion under its premises; a single positive example or a failed check cannot establish the universal law.

assumptions: k is an arbitrary natural number, including zero; p and q are arbitrary real-coefficient polynomials, including the zero polynomial.
For every natural j with 0≤j≤k, the j-th ordinary derivatives of p and q agree at -1 and also agree at 0.
Both p and q have degree at most 2k+2 under the stated zero-polynomial convention.
conventions: Real polynomials and ordinary derivatives; the zero polynomial is allowed and satisfies the nonnegative degree bounds.
items.question: Proposition P: for every natural number k and all real-coefficient polynomials p and q, if both have degree at most 2k+2, and all their ordinary derivatives of orders 0 through k agree at -1 and agree at 0, then p=q. Is P valid under the assumptions and conventions below?
items.reference_answer: P is invalid. For every natural k and every nonzero real c, choose p(x)=c*x^(k+1)*(x+1)^(k+1) and q(x)=0. The polynomial p is nonzero and has exact degree2k+2 because its leading coefficient is c. Each endpoint is a root of multiplicity at least k+1, so every derivative of order0 through k vanishes at both-1 and0. Hence p and q satisfy both degree bounds and both endpoint jet-equality hypotheses, but p≠q. Already k=0,c=1 gives p=x(x+1),q=0. The degree allowance2k+2 permits a nonzero multiple of the two endpoint multiplicity factors; divisibility and coprimality still hold. Restoring both bounds to2k+1 repairs universal uniqueness. More precisely, at allowance2k+2 any two polynomials with equal jets differ by a constant multiple of x^(k+1)*(x+1)^(k+1); the parameterized counterexample exhibits this missing freedom. That final classification is explanatory mathematics, not an additional certified root in this packet.

rubric.criterion: Respects arbitrary real polynomials, natural k including0, both degree bounds, exactly endpoints-1/0 and ordinary derivatives j=0..k.
Checks every required endpoint derivative equality for the chosen counterexample and k, by direct computation, justified multiplicity or an equivalent argument.
Verifies the allowed degree bounds and non-equality, and explains the role of the extra degree. A single admissible exact witness is sufficient; an all-k family is an additional valid route.
Uses an exact admissible counterexample and respects the scope of the negated universal statement; neither a compiler failure nor a claim that every instance fails is a substitute.
